mainTopic: Whose תחום objects follow on יום טוב (gifts, deposits, hung meat), and which animals are מוקצה for slaughter
overview: The משנה rules that guests may not carry home food their host gave them on יום טוב unless he transferred ownership to them on ערב יום טוב, because an object follows the תחום of whoever owned it when יום טוב began. The גמרא brings a מחלוקת: רב says deposited produce follows the person holding it, and שמואל says it follows the owner. The גמרא tries to tie this to their rulings in a damages dispute between חכמים and רבי, but each of them shows that his view stands on its own. The גמרא then defends רב against two challenges from the משנה. It answers that a corner set aside for the owner, or a full transfer of ownership, is not an ordinary deposit. Next comes a story about meat that רב חנא בר חנילאי hung on his host's door bar. After several challenges, the גמרא explains רב הונא's ruling as being about meat left unwatched, not about תחומין. A new משנה then teaches that only animals that sleep in town may be watered and slaughtered on יום טוב, and the גמרא explains why watering is mentioned. A ברייתא defines desert and town animals, with רבי giving a narrower definition. The גמרא begins to ask whether רבי accepts מוקצה at all, and that discussion continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Guests cannot carry home the host's portions
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that guests may not carry away the portions their host gave them on יום טוב, unless he transferred ownership to them before יום טוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone invited guests to his home, they may not carry portions of food home in their hands. This is permitted only if he transferred ownership of their portions to them on ערב יום טוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה rules on guests who come from another town for יום טוב. They may not take home the food the host hands them unless it became theirs before יום טוב began.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On יום טוב an object may only travel as far as its owner may walk. It is כרגלי the owner, meaning it is tied to the owner's feet. The food belonged to the host when יום טוב began, so it stays within the host's תחום even after he gives it away. If he made it theirs on ערב יום טוב through זכייה, it follows their feet instead.

keyTerms.meaning: Guests
Portions of food
Transferred ownership (often through a third party)
The day before the festival

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole סוגיא. On יום טוב, the status of an object depends on who owned it when the festival began.

phrases.english: One who invited guests to his home —
phrases.notes: The guests came from beyond his תחום, using an עירוב תחומין.

phrases.english: they may not carry portions in their hands (back home),
unless he transferred ownership to them of
their portions from the day before the festival.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שֶׁזִּמֵּן אֶצְלוֹ אוֹרְחִים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Gifts given on יום טוב remain כרגלי the giver unless ownership was transferred on ערב יום טוב.

steps.title: רב and שמואל disagree about deposited produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a מחלוקת about produce left with someone for safekeeping. רב says it follows the holder's feet, and שמואל says it follows the owner's feet.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: if someone deposits produce with his friend, רב said it goes like the feet of the person it was deposited with. שמואל said it goes like the feet of the depositor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a new case, a פיקדון. רב and שמואל disagree about whose תחום the deposited produce follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, ownership was clear: the host owned the food. Here the owner and the holder are different people. רב treats the watchman as the one in control. שמואל says ownership alone decides.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a dispute between אמוראים)
The one who deposits an item
Like the feet of; follows the תחום of

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was stated:
One who deposits produce with his fellow —

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: כְּרַגְלֵי מִי שֶׁהִפְקִידוּ לוֹ,
phrases.english: Rav said: like the feet of the one with whom they were deposited,
and Shmuel said: like the feet of the depositor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר: הַמַּפְקִיד פֵּירוֹת אֵצֶל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the משנה's principle (objects follow the owner) to a case where the owner and the holder differ.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: deposited produce follows the watchman. שמואל: it follows the owner.

steps.title: Proposing a link to a damages dispute
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests רב and שמואל are following their known reasoning, and quotes a משנה where חכמים and רבי disagree about a courtyard owner's liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say רב and שמואל follow their own reasoning? We learned: if someone brought things into another's courtyard with permission, the courtyard owner is liable. רבי says he is never liable unless the homeowner accepts on himself to watch them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a comparison. It quotes a משנה about damages that it will link to רב and שמואל in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to חכמים, giving permission to bring something into your courtyard is enough to make you responsible for it. According to רבי, you are responsible only if you explicitly agreed to watch it. The question is whether the תחום dispute mirrors this one.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say (introduces a suggested link)
They follow their own line of reasoning
With permission
The owner of the courtyard
To guard / watch

steps.confusionAlert: The first opinion in this quoted משנה ("the courtyard owner is liable") is the view of the חכמים, not רבי. רבי is the one who requires an explicit agreement to guard.

phrases.english: Shall we say that Rav and Shmuel
follow their own reasoning,
as we learned: If he brought (items) in with permission —
the courtyard owner is liable.
Rabbi says: he is never liable

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיְּקַבֵּל עָלָיו בַּעַל הַבַּיִת לִשְׁמוֹר.
phrases.english: unless the homeowner accepts upon himself to guard.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל דְּאָזְדוּ לְטַעְמַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Seeks a deeper source for the רב and שמואל dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the תחום dispute just an application of the חכמים and רבי dispute about a courtyard owner's responsibility?

steps.title: רב and שמואל's rulings complete the link
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא reports that רב ruled like חכמים and שמואל ruled like רבי, so the גמרא proposes that each one's תחום view follows from his ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said in the name of רב: the הלכה follows the חכמים. שמואל said: the הלכה follows רבי. Shall we say רב spoke like the רבנן and שמואל spoke like רבי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב and שמואל already took sides in the damages dispute. It then proposes that their תחום positions match those sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב follows חכמים, so permission alone makes the holder responsible, and therefore the produce follows the holder's feet. שמואל follows רבי, so the holder has no real connection to the item, and therefore it follows the owner. The parallel looks neat.

keyTerms.meaning: The binding law follows
The Sages (same as חכמים)

phrases.english: And Rav Huna said that Rav said:
The halakha follows the words of the Sages,
and Shmuel said: The halakha follows Rabbi.
Shall we say Rav spoke like the Rabbis
and Shmuel spoke like Rabbi?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב: הֲלָכָה כְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the data that connects רב and שמואל to the quoted משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That the תחום dispute between רב and שמואל depends on the חכמים and רבי dispute.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב הונא's report of how רב and שמואל ruled on the courtyard משנה.

steps.title: רב's view works even according to רבי
steps.stepSummary: רב rejects the link. רבי exempts the courtyard owner only because normally nobody agrees to guard, but a person who accepts a deposit has agreed to guard it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב can tell you: I said my view even according to רבי. רבי only said his view there, because in an ordinary case the homeowner did not take on guarding. But here, he did take on guarding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proposed link. רב can hold his view about the deposit even if he followed רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's condition is accepting responsibility to guard. Permission to use a courtyard does not usually include that, but taking a פיקדון does. So the deposit case meets even רבי's standard, and the item follows the watchman's feet.

keyTerms.meaning: He can say to you (defends a position)
He only said his view up to here (limits a ruling)
In an ordinary, unspecified case
Guarding / responsibility to watch

steps.whatToRemember: A פיקדון automatically includes accepting the job of guarding, so רב's view (the item follows the watchman) fits even רבי's opinion.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that accepting a שמירה obligation can link an object to the watchman for תחום purposes, separate from who owns it.

phrases.english: Rav can say to you:
I said it even according to Rabbi —

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי הָתָם,
phrases.english: Rabbi only said his view there
because in an ordinary case
he did not accept upon himself guarding,
but here —
he did accept upon himself guarding.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַב: אֲנָא דַּאֲמַרִי אֲפִילּוּ לְרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proposed link between רב's view and חכמים.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the claim that רב must follow חכמים. The rulings themselves stand.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The comparison ignores that a פיקדון includes accepting the job of guarding, which satisfies רבי's condition.

steps.title: שמואל also separates his view from the courtyard debate
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says his view works even according to the רבנן. The רבנן made the courtyard owner responsible only because the ox's owner is happy to have his ox count as being in the courtyard owner's domain. Nobody wants his produce to count as being in someone else's domain for תחום.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: My ruling works even according to the רבנן. The רבנן said what they said there only because a person is happy for his ox to count as being in the courtyard owner's domain, so that if it causes damage there, he does not have to pay. But here, is a person happy for his produce to count as being in his friend's domain?!
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל does what רב did in the step before. He shows that his ruling on תחום does not have to come from his ruling in the courtyard debate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the courtyard case, it helps the ox's owner if the courtyard owner counts as the guard. Then he does not pay for damage his ox does there. In the תחום case it does not help the produce's owner to have it count as someone else's. It would only stop him from carrying it, so even the רבנן would agree it follows the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: It suits him / he is happy with it
His ox
The courtyard owner
His domain / his responsibility
Causes damage

steps.whatToRemember: Both רב and שמואל cut the link between the two debates. The courtyard-damages debate and the deposit-תחום debate stand on their own.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two sides. רב (holder's feet) had been linked to the רבנן, and שמואל (owner's feet) to רבי. Here שמואל is showing that even the רבנן could agree with him.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
What I said holds even according to the Rabbis —

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָתָם,
phrases.english: The Rabbis only said their ruling there
because a person is happy
for his ox to stand
in the domain of the courtyard owner,
so that if it damages him, he is not liable.
phrases.notes: Once the courtyard owner took on guarding, the ox's owner is free from paying for damage there.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא — מִי נִיחָא לֵיהּ לְאִינִישׁ
phrases.english: But here — is a person happy
for his produce to stand in his friend's domain?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: אֲנָא דַּאֲמַרִי אֲפִילּוּ לְרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors רב's rejection in step 5, now from שמואל's side.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proposed link between שמואל's תחום view and the view of רבי in the courtyard case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The רבנן's reason in the courtyard case (the ox's owner gains from it) does not apply to תחום, where the owner gains nothing.

steps.title: Challenge to רב from the עירוב case
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that if the owner made an עירוב, his produce goes where he can go. If the produce follows the holder, how would the owner's עירוב matter?
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: 'And if he made an עירוב, his produce is like him.' But if you say the produce follows the feet of the person it was left with, what difference does the owner's עירוב make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's view using a line from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ties the produce to the owner's עירוב, which suggests the produce follows the owner. Under רב, the produce should follow the holder, so the owner's עירוב should not matter.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned (in a משנה)
He made an עירוב (extending his תחום)
Like the feet of: it may go only where that person may go
What difference does it make?

phrases.english: We learned: And if he made an eruv —
his produce is like him.
And if you say
it is like the feet of the one with whom it was deposited,
when he (the owner) made an eruv, what difference does it make?

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: וְאִם עֵרַב הוּא פֵּירוֹתָיו כָּמוֹהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both links are cut, the גמרא now tests רב's view directly against the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a deposit follows the holder's feet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה makes the owner's עירוב decide where the produce can go. That only makes sense if the produce follows the owner.

steps.title: The holder set aside a corner for the owner
steps.stepSummary: The school of רב answers that the משנה is speaking of a case where the holder set aside a special corner for the owner's produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said in the name of the school of רב: The משנה means a case where the holder set aside a corner for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The students of רב defend him by narrowing the case in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Setting aside a corner shows the holder never took the produce into his own domain. It still counts as the owner's, so it follows the owner's feet and his עירוב. In a normal deposit, רב's rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: They said in the school of רב
Set aside / designated
A corner

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא, אָמְרִי בֵּי רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Huna said, they said in the school of Rav:
For example, where he set aside a corner for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא, אָמְרִי בֵּי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to describe an ordinary deposit following the owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is a special case where a corner was set aside, so the produce never entered the holder's domain.

steps.title: Challenge to רב from the guests case
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה says guests may carry their portions home if the host gave them ownership before יום טוב. If items follow the holder, the food is still in the host's house, so why would that help?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Someone who invited guests: they may not carry portions home in their hands unless he gave them ownership of their portions before יום טוב. But if you say items follow the feet of the one they were left with, what difference does it make if he gave them ownership through someone else?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second challenge against רב, from the משנה of our דף (step 1).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even after the guests get ownership, the food stays in the host's house. Under רב's rule it should follow the host. The משנה, however, lets the guests take it, which looks like it follows the owners.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (a source is brought)
Gave ownership
Through another person
Portions

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: מִי שֶׁזִּמֵּן אֶצְלוֹ אוֹרְחִים —
phrases.english: Come and hear: One who invited guests to him —
they may not carry portions in their hands,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן זִכָּה לָהֶם מָנוֹתֵיהֶם
phrases.english: unless he gave them ownership of their portions
from the eve of the Festival.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ כְּרַגְלֵי מִי שֶׁהִפְקִידוֹ אֶצְלוֹ,
phrases.english: And if you say it is like the feet of the one with whom it was deposited,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי זִכָּה לָהֶם עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר

what difference does it make?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מִי שֶׁזִּמֵּן אֶצְלוֹ אוֹרְחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רב from the משנה, after the first was answered.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that a deposit follows the holder.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The portions stay in the host's house, yet the guests may carry them. That suggests the portions follow their owners, not the holder.

steps.title: Giving ownership counts like setting aside a corner
steps.stepSummary: Giving the guests ownership through another person counts the same as setting aside a corner for them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too: since he gave them ownership through another person, it is like setting aside a corner for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the guests challenge with the same idea it used for the עירוב case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By formally handing the portions to the guests, the host shows he is not holding them as his own. So the food counts as being in the guests' domain and follows their feet. רב's rule for a normal deposit is untouched.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too / so too
Is like / is compared to

phrases.english: Here too,

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁזִּכָּה לָהֶם עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר —
phrases.english: since he gave them ownership through another person —

phrases.aramaic: כְּמִי שֶׁיִּחֵד לוֹ קֶרֶן זָוִית דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: it is like one who set aside a corner for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי, כֵּיוָן שֶׁזִּכָּה לָהֶם עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by using the 'corner' idea from step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The portions stayed in the host's house, so they should follow the host.
steps.terutzMaskana: Giving ownership counts as setting aside a corner, so the portions follow the guests.

steps.title: A second answer: giving ownership is different
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: a case of giving ownership (זיכה) is simply different from an ordinary deposit.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: giving ownership is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second, separate answer to the guests challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not need the 'corner' idea. When a host gives his guests full ownership on purpose, he clearly means the portions to be theirs in every way. So they follow the guests' feet, which is unlike a plain deposit that the holder agreed to guard.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (a second answer)
Is different

steps.whatToRemember: רב's rule (a deposit follows the holder's feet) survives both challenges. The משנה's cases are exceptions: either the holder set aside a corner, or he gave full ownership. Neither is an ordinary deposit.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: transferring ownership is different.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: זִכָּה שָׁאנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 9, given alongside step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Giving ownership would still leave the portions as a deposit in the host's house.
steps.terutzMaskana: Giving ownership is its own category. The host fully means the portions to belong to the guests, so they follow the guests.

steps.title: רב הונא rules on the meat hung on the door bar
steps.stepSummary: רב חנא בר חנילאי hung meat on his host's door bar. רב הונא ruled he may take it if he hung it himself, but not if the hosts hung it for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנא בר חנילאי hung meat on the bar of the door. He came before רב הונא, who said to him: If you hung it, go take it. But if they hung it for you, do not take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life story that tests the rule from the previous steps about whose "feet" an item follows. רב הונא gives a two-part ruling based on who hung the meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On יום טוב, an item can only be carried where its "owner" may walk. רב הונא says the meat follows רב חנא if he hung it himself. If the hosts hung it, it follows the hosts and must stay put. Both halves of this ruling will now be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: he hung
meat
the bar or beam of the door
go take it

phrases.english: Rav Chana bar Chanilai
hung meat on the bar of the door.
phrases.notes: This was in his host's house, outside his own town.

phrases.english: He came before Rav Huna,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי אַתְּ תְּלֵית — זִיל שְׁקֵיל,
phrases.english: he said to him: If you hung it, go take it,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אִינְהוּ תְּלוֹ לָךְ — לָא תִּשְׁקוֹל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a practical story that applies the concepts of deposit and a set-aside corner.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat a guest hung himself follows the guest. Meat the hosts hung for him does not follow him.

steps.title: How can he take it if רב says deposits follow the holder
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא was a student of רב, and רב said a deposited item follows the person holding it. So even if רב חנא hung the meat himself, it should follow the host.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he hung it himself, may he take it? But רב הונא was a student of רב, and רב said: it is like the feet of the one with whom it was deposited!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first half of רב הונא's ruling. It argues that his own teacher רב would not let רב חנא take the meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's rule is that a deposit follows the holder, which here is the host. The meat sat in the host's house, so it should be limited to where the host may walk. A student would not normally rule against his teacher.

keyTerms.meaning: student
like the feet of (it may go wherever this person may walk)
the one with whom it was deposited (the holder)

phrases.english: And if he himself hung it, may he take it?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא רַב הוּנָא תַּלְמִיד דְּרַב הֲוָה,
phrases.english: But Rav Huna was a student of Rav,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב: כְּרַגְלֵי מִי שֶׁהִפְקִידוּ אֶצְלוֹ!
phrases.english: and Rav said: it is like the feet of the one with whom it was deposited!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא רַב הוּנָא תַּלְמִיד דְּרַב הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the first half of רב הונא's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that if רב חנא hung the meat himself he may take it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב, רב הונא's teacher, rules that a deposit follows the holder. So the meat should follow the host no matter who hung it.

steps.title: A door bar is like a corner set aside for him
steps.stepSummary: A door bar is different. Hanging something there is like the host setting aside a corner for the guest, so the meat stays his.
steps.simpleTranslation: A door bar is different, because it is like a case of one who set aside a corner for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the door bar counts as the guest's own special spot. It uses the "set-aside corner" idea from step 8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's rule covers an ordinary deposit mixed into the host's home. A distinct spot like a door bar belongs to the guest, just like a special corner. So the meat follows רב חנא's feet, and his own עירוב lets him take it home.

keyTerms.meaning: it is different
a corner
that he set aside for him

phrases.english: The bar of the door is different,

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְמִי שֶׁיִּחֵד לוֹ קֶרֶן זָוִית דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: since it is like one who set aside a corner for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי עִבְרָא דְּדָשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the case: a door bar is an exception to רב's ordinary deposit rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Meat in the host's house is an ordinary deposit that follows the host.
steps.terutzMaskana: A door bar is a designated spot like a set-aside corner, so the meat follows the guest.

steps.title: שמואל's fattened ox suggests the meat should follow him
steps.stepSummary: רב הלל asks: why can't he take it if the hosts hung it? שמואל said a fattener's ox follows whoever buys it. Likewise, meat meant for רב חנא should follow him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הלל said to רב אשי: And if they hung it for him, may he not take it? But שמואל said: the ox of a fattener is like the feet of every person!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא turns to challenge the second half of רב הונא's ruling. This is the first of three challenges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fattener's ox is meant for any buyer, so it follows whoever buys it on יום טוב. This shows an item can follow the person it was meant for. The meat was clearly meant for רב חנא, so it should follow him even if the hosts hung it.

keyTerms.meaning: an ox of a fattener (raised to be sold for meat)
like the feet of every person (it follows whoever buys it)
he may not take

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הִלֵּל לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Hillel said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אִינְהוּ תָּלוּ לֵיהּ לָא שָׁקֵיל?
phrases.english: And if they hung it for him, may he not take it?
But didn't Shmuel say:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁל פַּטָּם — הֲרֵי הוּא כְּרַגְלֵי כׇּל אָדָם.
phrases.english: An ox of a fattener is like the feet of every person.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אִינְהוּ תָּלוּ לֵיהּ לָא שָׁקֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first half of the ruling to attack the second half.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that if the hosts hung the meat, רב חנא may not take it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל shows an item can follow the person it is meant for. The meat was meant for רב חנא, so it should follow him.

steps.title: The הלכה follows רבי דוסא
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks the same question. רבי יוחנן ruled like רבי דוסא that an animal surely going to the town's only shepherd follows the shepherd. So meat surely meant for רב חנא should follow him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: And if they hung it for him, may he not take it? But רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: the הלכה follows רבי דוסא!
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second challenge to the same half of רב הונא's ruling, from a different source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי דוסא holds that in a town with only one shepherd, the animals follow the shepherd's feet. This is because they will certainly be handed to him. Since the hosts clearly set the meat aside for רב חנא, it should likewise follow him.

keyTerms.meaning: the halacha follows
Tanna who holds an animal certain to go to the only shepherd follows the shepherd

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אִינְהוּ תָּלוּ לֵיהּ לָא שָׁקֵיל?
phrases.english: And if they hung it for him, may he not take it?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: But didn't Rabba bar bar Chana say in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
The halacha follows Rabbi Dosa.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel second challenge to the same ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that if the hosts hung the meat, רב חנא may not take it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under רבי דוסא, an item certain to reach a person follows that person. The meat was certainly meant for רב חנא.

steps.title: The משנה says animals and vessels follow their owner
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks רב כהנא the same question. A משנה says animals and vessels follow their owner. The meat belongs to רב חנא, so it should follow him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to רב כהנא: And if they hung it for him, may he not take it? But we learned in a משנה: animals and vessels are like the feet of the owners!
steps.whatsHappening: This is the third challenge to the second half of רב הונא's ruling, this time from a משנה. The next step (step 18) answers all these challenges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic rule in the משנה is that items follow their owner. The meat was given to רב חנא as his, so it should follow his feet. It should not matter who physically hung it.

keyTerms.meaning: but we learned in a משנה
animals and vessels
the owners

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא allowed taking the meat only if רב חנא hung it himself, because the door bar works like a set-aside corner. Three challenges (שמואל, רבי דוסא, the משנה) argue that he should be allowed to take it even if the hosts hung it.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two halves. Step 13 asked why he CAN take it. Steps 15-17 ask why he CANNOT take it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to Rav Kahana:

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אִינְהוּ תָּלוּ לֵיהּ לָא שָׁקֵיל?
phrases.english: And if they hung it for him, may he not take it?
But didn't we learn in a mishnah:
Animals and vessels are like the feet of the owners!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתְנַן הַבְּהֵמָה וְהַכֵּלִים כְּרַגְלֵי הַבְּעָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third parallel challenge to the same ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that if the hosts hung the meat, רב חנא may not take it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says items follow their owner. The meat is רב חנא's, so it should follow him regardless of who hung it.

steps.title: A new explanation: the meat question was about leaving it unwatched
steps.stepSummary: Because of all the questions, the גמרא changes how it reads the story. רב חנא is a busy scholar. If he hung the meat himself, he knows its sign and kept his mind on it, so he may take it. If the hosts hung it for him, his mind was off it, so he may not take it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב חנא בר חנילאי is different. He is a great man who is busy with his learning. This is what רב הונא told him: If you hung it yourself, you know a sign on it and your mind never left it, so go take it. But if they hung it for you, your mind left it, so do not take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its earlier reading of the story, because the three questions in steps 15–17 had no answer under that reading. It explains the ruling as being about meat that went unwatched, not about whose 'place' the meat belongs to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All the questions assumed the issue was which person's תחומין the meat follows. Now the issue is different: meat that was out of sight might have been swapped for non-kosher meat. If רב חנא hung it, he knows its sign, so it is safe. If the hosts hung it, he never paid attention to it, so it counts as unwatched meat.

keyTerms.meaning: Is different. Used to show that a case is an exception to the usual rule.
Busy with his learning, so his mind is on his studies.
A sign or mark that lets you recognize something.
You took your mind off it. You stopped paying attention to it.
Meat that was out of sight and unwatched, and may have been swapped for forbidden meat.

steps.whatToRemember: Steps 13–17 asked about תחומין, and none of those questions apply anymore. רב הונא's ruling was really about meat left unwatched. Whether רב חנא may take it depends on whether he himself kept track of it.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not keep reading this step as a תחומין ruling. The word אלא tells you the גמרא has switched to a completely different topic: unwatched meat.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer settles the three remaining questions at once. It changes what topic the story is about, instead of fixing each question one by one.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, שָׁאנֵי רַב חָנָא בַּר חֲנִילַאי —
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Chana bar Chanilai is different —
phrases.notes: אלא signals that the earlier reading is dropped.

phrases.english: for he is a great man
and occupied with his learning,
phrases.notes: So he would not normally notice details about the meat.

phrases.english: and this is what he (Rav Huna) said to him:
if you hung it,
you have a recognizable sign on it
and you did not take your mind off it,
go take it.
But if they hung it for you,
you took your mind off it, and do not take it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, שָׁאנֵי רַב חָנָא בַּר חֲנִילַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the three unanswered questions from steps 15–17 by changing what the case is about. The earlier answer in step 14 is no longer needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the case. The topic changes from תחומין to meat left unwatched.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רב הונא's ruling was about which person's תחומין the meat follows.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling is about unwatched meat. רב חנא may take it only if he hung it himself and knows its sign.

steps.title: New משנה: desert animals vs. town animals on יום טוב
steps.stepSummary: On יום טוב, you may not water and slaughter מדבריות, but you may water and slaughter בייתות. בייתות are animals that sleep in town. מדבריות are animals that sleep in the pasture.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: We do not water and slaughter desert animals. But we do water and slaughter house animals. House animals are those that sleep in the town. Desert animals are those that sleep in the pasture.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts here. It teaches which animals may be slaughtered on יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מדבריות live out in the pasture, so before יום טוב nobody planned to use them. They are מוקצה and may not be slaughtered. בייתות sleep in town, so they are ready to be used.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה.
Desert animals. They live out in the pasture.
House animals. They sleep in town.
We give water to (the animals).
Open pasture land outside the town.
Set aside from use, so it may not be used on שבת or יום טוב.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְנִי׳ אֵין מַשְׁקִין וְשׁוֹחֲטִין אֶת הַמִּדְבָּרִיּוֹת,
phrases.english: MISHNA: We do not water and slaughter desert animals,
but we do water and slaughter domestic animals.
These are domestic animals — those that sleep in the town.
Desert animals — those that sleep in the pasture.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין מַשְׁקִין וְשׁוֹחֲטִין אֶת הַמִּדְבָּרִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה. It is not connected to the רב חנא discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On יום טוב, only animals that sleep in town may be watered and slaughtered. Pasture animals are מוקצה.

steps.title: Why does the משנה mention watering?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה needed to say 'water and slaughter.' The topic is slaughtering, so why mention watering?
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why do I need the משנה to say 'water and slaughter'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the wording of the משנה. It sets up the answer that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is about which animals are מוקצה for slaughtering. Watering seems to have nothing to do with that. So the extra word needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה.
Why do I need it? Asked when a word seems extra.
To say.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Why do I need [the Mishna] to say
'we water and slaughter'?

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמָה לִי לְמֵימַר מַשְׁקִין וְשׁוֹחֲטִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the משנה mentions watering when its topic is slaughtering.

steps.title: A side lesson: water the animal before slaughtering
steps.stepSummary: The משנה slips in a practical tip. Water your animal before you slaughter it, because then the skin comes off the meat more easily.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us something on the side: a person should water his animal first and then slaughter it, because otherwise the skin sticks to the meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The word 'water' is there to teach a useful practical lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The watering is not part of the מוקצה rule. It teaches good practice: if the animal drinks before slaughter, it is easier to skin afterward.

keyTerms.meaning: A lesson taught on the side, along the way.
It teaches us.
The skin sticking to the meat.
And afterward.

phrases.aramaic: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן,
phrases.english: It teaches us a matter incidentally,
that a person should water his animal
and afterward slaughter it,
because of the skin sticking (to the meat).

steps.triggerLanguage: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'water' teaches a practical tip: water the animal before slaughter so the skin comes off easily.

steps.title: ברייתא: how to define desert animals and house animals
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says מדבריות go out to pasture at פסח time and only come back at the first rain. בייתות go out to graze, even beyond the תחום, but come back to sleep inside the תחום.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Which are desert animals and which are house animals? Desert animals are any that go out at פסח time, graze in the pasture, and come back at the first rainfall. House animals are any that go out and graze outside the תחום, but come back and sleep inside the תחום.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא gives exact definitions for the two kinds of animals in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What decides the category is where the animal sleeps. Grazing far away, even outside the תחום, still counts as בייתות if the animal comes back each night. Only animals that stay out the whole summer count as מדבריות.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. This introduces a ברייתא.
At פסח time, the start of the dry season.
The first rainfall of the rainy season.
The boundary around a town, past which you may not walk on שבת or יום טוב.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that grazing outside the תחום makes an animal a מדבריות. What matters is that it comes back to sleep inside the תחום.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: אֵלּוּ הֵן מִדְבָּרִיּוֹת וְאֵלּוּ הֵן בַּיָּיתוֹת.
phrases.english: Which are desert animals and which are domestic animals?
Desert animals — all that go out at Passover time
and graze in the pasture,
and come in at the first rainfall.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵלּוּ הֵן בַּיָּיתוֹת — כֹּל שֶׁיּוֹצְאוֹת וְרוֹעוֹת חוּץ לַתְּחוּם,
phrases.english: And these are domestic animals — all that go out and graze outside the boundary,
but come and sleep within the boundary.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵלּוּ הֵן מִדְבָּרִיּוֹת וְאֵלּוּ הֵן בַּיָּיתוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives exact definitions for the terms used in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מדבריות stay in the pasture from פסח until the first rain. בייתות come back each night to sleep inside the תחום.

steps.title: רבי's narrower definition of desert animals
steps.stepSummary: רבי says both groups count as בייתות. For him, only animals that never come into town, not in summer and not in winter, are מדבריות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי says: Both of these are house animals. Rather, desert animals are those that go out and graze in the pasture and never come into the town, not in the summer and not in the rainy season.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי disagrees with the first opinion in the ברייתא. He makes the group of מדבריות much smaller.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animals that stay out all summer still come home for the winter, so רבי treats them as town animals and allows them to be slaughtered. Only animals that never come into town at all are מוקצה. So רבי allows more animals to be slaughtered on יום טוב.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יהודה הנשיא.
The settled area, the town.
The summer (dry) season.
The rainy season.

steps.whatToRemember: The first opinion: an animal that stays out from פסח until the first rain is a מדבריות. רבי: only an animal that never comes into town at all is a מדבריות. Everything else is בייתות and may be slaughtered on יום טוב.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: אֵלּוּ וְאֵלּוּ בַּיָּיתוֹת הֵן.
phrases.english: Rabbi says: Both these and those are domestic animals.
Rather, these are desert animals —
all that go out and graze in the pasture,
and do not enter the settled area,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא בִּימוֹת הַחַמָּה וְלֹא בִּימוֹת הַגְּשָׁמִים.
phrases.english: neither in the summer nor in the rainy season.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: אֵלּוּ וְאֵלּוּ בַּיָּיתוֹת הֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion in the ברייתא and gives a narrower definition of מדבריות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only animals that never come into town, in any season, are מדבריות and מוקצה.

steps.title: Does רבי accept מוקצה at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי's view on מדבריות. Forbidding those animals assumes מוקצה. But רבי once told his son that according to רבי שמעון there is no מוקצה, as in the case of unripe dates set aside to ripen.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי really hold of מוקצה? But רבי שמעון the son of רבי asked רבי: 'Unripe dates put away to ripen, what is the law according to רבי שמעון?' He answered him: 'There is no מוקצה according to רבי שמעון'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי's ruling about מדבריות. It asks whether רבי accepts the idea of מוקצה at all, and brings an earlier conversation as its evidence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 23, רבי forbade slaughtering animals that never come into town. The reason is that they are מוקצה, meaning the owner did not have them in mind for use on יום טוב. But רבי told his son that רבי שמעון does not accept מוקצה, even for unripe dates that the owner has clearly put out of his mind. The full quote, and the reason this conversation creates a contradiction for רבי himself, continue right on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Set aside. Something a person did not have in mind to use on שבת or יום טוב, so it may not be used then.
"And does he really hold...?" A challenge opener that questions whether a sage holds a certain view.
"But surely..." Introduces the source that contradicts the claim.
He asked him. Introduces a question one person put to another.
Unripe dates. They are placed in a basket to ripen and are not yet edible.

steps.confusionAlert: The quote stops in the middle. Do not decide from this passage alone that רבי rejects מוקצה. So far, רבי is only reporting רבי שמעון's view. The next lines explain why this is a problem for רבי's own ruling.

phrases.english: And does Rabbi hold of muktzeh?
phrases.notes: This challenges רבי's ruling in step 23 that מדבריות are forbidden.

phrases.english: But surely he asked him
Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi asked of Rabbi:
Unripe dates (put away to ripen) —
phrases.notes: They are not edible yet, so the owner has put them out of mind.

phrases.english: according to Rabbi Shimon, what is the law?
phrases.notes: This refers to רבי שמעון בן יוחאי, not רבי's son.

phrases.english: He said to him:
There is no muktzeh according to Rabbi Shimon
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִית לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי מוּקְצֶה? וְהָא בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This challenges the reasoning behind רבי's definition of מדבריות in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's ruling that animals which never come into town (מדבריות) may not be slaughtered on יום טוב, which assumes the law of מוקצה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי told his son that רבי שמעון does not accept מוקצה, even for dates set aside to ripen. The גמרא is setting up a conflict between that answer and רבי's own ruling. The full argument finishes on the next amud.
